rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient to elute all 10 compounds and map the elution window without much risk of truncation. This should reveal whether peaks are compressed early, late, or across the full gradient so later runs can trim the window and adjust slope.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the next gain is reducing t_last by trimming the gradient window toward the observed elution window and shortening the run. The last peak eluted during the gradient at about phi_e ~0.59, so setting phi1 to 0.60 and a shorter tG should test whether we can pull the run under 10 minutes while preserving resolution.

Since changing the gradient window and slope barely moved retention, temperature is the most promising lever to cut t_last below 10 minutes while likely keeping all pairs resolved. This run probes whether a 10 C increase gives a substantial global retention drop without collapsing the closest mid-run pair.

At 50 C the critical pair catastrophically coeluted, so the best direction is to bracket the temperature effect with a smaller increase from 40 C. This tests whether we can gain some time reduction while keeping the sensitive pair above baseline resolution.

The 45 C run suggests temperature can shorten the analysis, but the key pair needs more gradient-derived spacing to recover full credit. Lengthening tG at the same phi window tests whether the critical pair is slope-responsive enough to restore R >= 1.5 while retaining some of the temperature-driven time gain.

The critical pair is highly temperature-sensitive but comfortably resolved at 40 C, and narrowing the window further should steepen the effective gradient and push the late peak out earlier if it is still eluting near the upper end of the solvent range. This checks whether we can shave last-peak time at 40 C without sacrificing the already adequate resolution.

Lowering phi1 made the last peak later, so the last compound is effectively sensitive to stronger final eluent rather than just gradient steepness. A modest increase to phi1 = 0.65 should pull the late peak earlier while keeping conditions close to the current best method and likely preserving full resolution.

The move to phi1 = 0.65 improved CRF by pulling the last peak earlier while retaining full resolution, so the next logical step is a small further increase in phi1. This tests whether the late peak can be shortened again without driving the current critical pair below R = 1.5.

We are close to the ideal 10-minute last peak and still have margin on the critical pair at phi1 = 0.70, so one more increase in phi1 is the best exploitation step. This should reveal whether we can push t_last to about 10 minutes while maintaining R >= 1.5 for the weakest pair.

At phi1 = 0.75 we are very close to optimal, but the critical pair has just slipped below full-credit resolution, so a slightly shallower gradient is the cleanest way to recover that pair. Increasing tG by one step should improve R(6,7) with only a modest penalty in t_last, testing for a net gain above the current best.

The best current method is limited only by a slight shortfall in the critical pair, so the next efficient probe is to raise phi0 one step while keeping the successful high phi1 and short tG. This changes the phi window rather than temperature or long-run slope and may improve selectivity for the close pair while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes.

We have already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000, so the only useful remaining objective is robustness mapping around the optimum. A small increase in phi1 tests how close the current method is to the edge of losing the critical pair while likely keeping the last peak under 10 minutes.

Since 0.10–0.75, 12 min at 40 C already achieves the maximum CRF, the best remaining question is whether the gradient can be shortened and still keep all pairs at R >= 1.5 with t_last under 10 min. This run probes whether a 10 min gradient preserves the critical pair or crosses the edge.

The optimum at 40 C is just above the resolution threshold for the critical pair, and lowering temperature should increase selectivity margin while likely still keeping t_last under 10 minutes. This maps robustness on the cool side and may reveal an equally optimal but more forgiving method.

Since the 40 C optimum is exact but fairly tight, a slightly lower phi1 than 0.75 should add resolution margin while still likely keeping t_last under 10 minutes thanks to the higher phi0. This is a direct robustness check around the optimum without changing temperature or gradient time.

The key discovery was that increasing phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 simultaneously improved the critical pair and pulled the run under 10 minutes, so one more step in phi0 is the most informative remaining local probe. This tests whether further trimming the low-organic end can keep all peaks resolved while shortening the run even more.

Moving phi0 from 0.10 to 0.15 preserved full score and shortened t_last further, so one more increase in phi0 is the highest-value local optimization test. This checks whether we can trim the front of the gradient again without pushing the first peak too close to unretained behavior or losing the critical mid-run pair.

The 0.15/0.75 method keeps full score with a bit more room than 0.20/0.75, so increasing phi1 one step from that safer baseline is the best local test for an even shorter fully resolved method. This will show whether we can gain speed at phi0 = 0.15 without dropping the critical pair below R = 1.5.

We already have two maximum-score methods, so the most useful remaining experiment is to map a more conservative variant of the better-trimmed 0.15/0.75 window. Increasing tG one step should reveal whether this setting offers extra resolution robustness around the critical pair while still remaining fully under the 10-minute time target.

A slightly lower phi1 from the successful 0.15/0.75 setting should improve the critical pair margin and may still remain below the 10-minute threshold, giving a potentially more robust maximum-score method. This is the cleanest unresolved local test around the best-trimmed window.

We have already identified 40 C as optimal for score, but with several injections left it is worth checking whether the better-trimmed 0.15/0.75 window behaves differently with temperature than the earlier 0.05/0.60 window did. This probes whether a hotter method can still keep the critical pair resolved while remaining well under 10 minutes.

Higher temperature strongly compresses the critical pair, so the only plausible way to rescue it at 45 C is a shallower gradient on the proven 0.10/0.75 window. This run tests whether slope can offset the temperature-induced collapse enough to regain full or near-full resolution while staying close to the time target.

With the optimum already found, the best use of a remaining shot is to probe an orthogonal corner of the local design space where lower temperature may separate the troublesome pair while the shorter gradient compensates for retention. This tests whether a distinct fully resolved fast method exists away from 40 C.

With two full-score methods already in hand, use a remaining shot to test for a more robust alternative by combining the safe lower phi1 with a slightly shallower gradient on the proven 40 C platform. This should increase resolution margin around the critical pair and shows whether the 10-minute threshold can still be met.

For the last unused shot, test the lower-phi1 edge of the successful phi0 = 0.15 family to complete the local map around the optimum. This should increase resolution margin further, and it will show whether that added margin can still keep the last peak at or near the 10-minute target.
